items.title: Morning Briefing: Oct. 27, 2026
items.excerpt: 27 October 2026• Update: 27 October 2026 WASHINGTON DC Here’s a rundown of all the news you need to start your Tuesday, including Israelis heading to polls in parliamentary elections, Russia-Ukraine ceasefire in Oleshky brokered by US first lady taking effect, Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Iran holding a quadrilateral meeting in Tehran, and Saudi-led coalition saying it intercepted and destroyed three ballistic missiles launched by Yemen’s Houthi group. Voting began Tuesday in Israel’s parliamentary elections, with more than 7.3 million people eligible to cast ballots to elect the 120-member Knesset. Polling stations opened at 7 am local time (0500GMT) and are scheduled to close at 10 pm (2000GMT), according to Israel’s Central Elections Committee. A total of 12,018 polling stations and approximately 18,000 ballot boxes have been prepared nationwide, with around 100,000 election workers deployed. Thirty-seven parties and electoral lists are competing in the elections, with at least 61 seats required to form a governing coalition. The main contenders include Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party, former Army Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party and the Together alliance led by former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett. The elections represent Israel’s first general vote since the start of its genocidal war on the Gaza Strip in October 2023. - Russia-Ukraine ceasefire in Oleshky brokered by US first lady takes effect A ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-controlled Ukrainian city of Oleshky brokered by US first lady Melania Trump took effect at 0100GMT on Tuesday to facilitate humanitarian aid deliveries and civilian evacuations. An official press release was issued Friday by the White House confirming that the first lady had served as the "Exclusive Intermediary" to secure the localized agreement. The development came amid worsening shortages of food, medicine and clean water in Oleshky, a frontline town located on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River in Ukraine's southern Kherson region. Residents must also contend with limited access to electricity, mined roads and recurring military attacks, according to the White House. - Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Iran hold quadrilateral meeting in Tehran A quadrilateral meeting between delegations from Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Iran began in the Iranian capital Tehran, with talks set to focus on regional security, Israel's activities in the region, and developments in Palestine and Lebanon. The meeting was hosted by Iran's Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei. Both Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi are attending, while Türkiye is represented by National Intelligence Organization (MIT) Director Ibrahim Kalin, Saudi Arabia by Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, and Pakistan by Chief of Army Staff Asim Munir. - Saudi-led coalition intercepts 3 Houthi ballistic missiles targeting kingdom’s east The Saudi-led coalition said its air defenses intercepted and destroyed three ballistic missiles launched by Yemen’s Houthi group toward Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province. The announcement did not specify the intended targets or provide details on possible casualties or damage. On Monday, the coalition said it intercepted and destroyed three drones over the Riyadh region and southern Saudi Arabia without identifying their origin or intended targets.

items.excerpt: Voters in Israel are deciding whether to oust Netanyahu after 3 years of war JERUSALEM (AP) — Israelis are voting in a pivotal election as the country grapples with unfinished wars and divisions over its future. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu voted just after midday. He faces a strong challenge from former military chief Gadi Eisenkot. Polls show neither candidate's party is likely to gain enough support for a parliamentary majority, leading to possibly weeks of negotiations over forming a winning coalition. The election is Israel's first national vote since the Oct. 7 attacks and serves as a referendum on Netanyahu's leadership. The outcome could shape Israel's identity as either more nationalist and religious or liberal democratic. ... MYKOLAIV, Ukraine (AP) — Finland's president and Norway's prime minister have spoken on the phone with Russian President ... The call was confirmed by the offices of Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb on Tuesday. It followed an Oct. 20 meeting in Oslo between the two Nordic leaders, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff. Officials said that the call was held in consultation with Ukraine. Stubb and Støre initiated the call to discuss the war and upcoming trilateral talks involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States that are expected to take place in United Arab Emirates in November. How Trump’s ‘little detour’ to Iran became a roadblock in the midterm elections WASHINGTON (AP) — When President Donald Trump launched his war on Iran, he said it would last a matter of weeks. Now, nearly eight months into it, rising energy costs and voter fatigue are weighing heavily on Republican candidates ahead of the midterm elections. An AP-NORC poll published last week found that voters from both major political parties want the next Congress to focus on making life more affordable and ending the war in Iran. But as the conflict grinds on, the situation in the Middle East has only become more complicated and is creating difficulties for Republicans making their case to voters. AP investigation: Documents support claim ICE has detained a mentally ill US citizen since January IOWA CITY, Iowa (AP) — An Associated Press review has found that for nearly a year immigration authorities have detained and sought to deport a mentally ill man whose mother, lawyers and public records say was born in the United States and not Jamaica as he claims. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has no authority to detain U.S. citizens, but has long done so, usually for hours or days, when officers mistake identities or can’t immediately verify citizenship. ICE's parent agency, the Department of Homeland Security, disputes that the man is a U.S. citizen and alleges, without providing evidence, that the birth certificate he submitted to obtain a U.S. passport that he held for 15 years was fraudulent. Congo’s Ebola outbreak tops 10,000 cases as authorities race to slow the spread in African countries BUNIA, Congo (AP) — Congo’s fast-moving Ebola outbreak has topped 10,000 confirmed cases as authorities race to slow the spread across Africa. Data from Congo's Ministry of Health on Tuesday showed there have been a total of 10,060 confirmed cases, nearly half of whom have died. It is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history and was declared in May. It is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. Response teams are battling armed conflict, poor roads and violence from residents fueled by mistrust and misinformation. It has spread farther across Africa than any previous Ebola outbreak, reaching three regions with cases recorded in Kenya and Nigeria as well.

items.title: Federal Reserve rate hikes are coming, but not this week: CNBC survey
items.excerpt: Published Tue, Oct 27 2026 7:10 AM EDT Steve Liesman@steveliesman Key Points - The CNBC Fed Survey shows that 93% of respondent expect a pause at the Federal Reserve meeting taking place this week - But 76% anticipate a rate hike at its next meeting in December. - More than half say the Fed will hike next year by an average of about two rate hikes. ... The Federal Reserve has considerable work to do. But it's not going to do it in October. That's the key finding in CNBC's latest Fed Survey of 30 fund managers, strategists and economists, which showed that 93% expect a pause at the Fed meeting taking place this week and 76% anticipate a rate hike at its next meeting in December. And more than half say the Fed will hike next year by an average of about two rate hikes. "Their hesitancy to raise rates is unfathomable after an extended period of monetary and fiscal generosity, with nominal GDP running 6-8%, and when the leading indicators of inflation are uniformly warm to hot,'' said Richard Bernstein, global head of macro investing at Janus Henderson Investors. A plurality of 40% say the Fed must slow growth below potential to solve the inflation problem. That compares with 27% who say the Fed does not need to slow the economy and 23% who say the Fed has to slow the economy only somewhat. The survey, which CNBC conducts before every Fed meeting, found that 70% see the inflation problem as broader than just the rising price of energy. The U.S. crude oil benchmark is forecast to be at $88 a barrel six months from now, up from $82 in the September survey, but below the current level of $101. Asked what the Fed should do at the current meeting, 30% said it should hike rates now. At least two Fed voters are expected by survey respondents to dissent from the decision to keep rates unchanged. "The aggregate demand data (probably north of 7%...) and the inflation data point to the strong need to hike rates,'' wrote John Ryding, chief economic advisor for Brean Capital, LLC. Not all agree. Some are concerned with a weakening economy. "The Iran War is intensifying, real wages are falling, interest rates are rising, and the AI-fueled stock market looks shaky," wrote Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics. "Inflation is high, but there's little sign it is becoming entrenched. This isn't the time for more Fed rate hikes. Amid numerous shocks and challenges — including high inflation, expected Fed rate hikes and a continuation of high oil prices — respondents still see economic growth remaining above potential, or the level of growth that doesn't lead to inflation or deflation. Forecasts of GDP for this year rose to 2.4%. They ticked down slightly since the last survey but still hover above potential at 2.2% for 2027. Growth in 2025 came in at 2.05%. Respondents in aggregate put the risk of the U.S. entering a recession in the next year at 26%, down from 29% in the last survey. ... Unemployment is forecast to remain steady at 4.2% through the remainder of the year but rise to 4.4% in 2027. The Consumer Price Index is seen ticking down to 3.6% from the current pace of 3.7% in September but fall meaningfully next year to 2.6%.

items.title: US stock futures muted as oil holds near April highs ahead of Fed decision By Reuters
items.excerpt: Oct 27 (Reuters) - US stock index futures ticked up on Tuesday as crude oil prices extended their decline, while investors awaited a slate of key corporate earnings and the Federal Reserve’s interest-rate decision this week. The Fed is widely expected to hold rates steady on Wednesday following an increase last month, though markets are pricing in at least two more hikes by mid-2027 as key inflation indicators remain elevated amid the ongoing US-Iran conflict. "While we don’t expect a rate move this week, we wouldn’t be against a hike even though we’re not convinced of its urgency," said John Velis, head of Americas Strategy at BNY. "We think maintaining credibility is paramount for the Fed, and as (Fed Chair Kevin) Warsh likes to remind us, the inflation target has been exceeded for well over 60 straight months." Brent crude slipped for the second straight day in volatile trading, though it still held near its highest level since late April.

Brent It follows talks between Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Pakistan and Iranian officials in Tehran on Monday, as they stepped up efforts to defuse tensions across the Middle East. Riyadh said the discussions were aimed at keeping diplomatic channels open and preventing another escalation in hostilities. The four countries agreed to continue to engage to advance regional peace and security, according to Iranian state media. The diplomatic push comes as U.S. President Donald Trump said in an interview with Fox News on Sunday that he was approaching a decision on whether to strike a deal with Iran or intensify military operations, suggesting that additional attacks remained an option. Representatives from Qatar, which has helped mediate negotiations between Washington and Tehran, also traveled to the Iranian capital on Sunday, Reuters reported. ... Prospects of a diplomatic breakthrough have helped temper fears of further disruptions to global energy supplies, putting downward pressure on crude prices. But earlier oil price losses were limited as the prospect of a lasting resolution appeared fragile, with Iran-backed Houthi militants continuing their attacks on Saudi Arabia over the weekend.

items.title: US business activity cools in October; strong demand fueling price pressures By Reuters
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON, Oct 23 (Reuters) - US business activity slowed modestly in October, though robust demand allowed companies to raise prices for goods and services, a sign that inflation could increase further and remain persistently high in the coming months. S&P Global said on Friday its flash US Composite PMI Output Index, which tracks the manufacturing and services sectors, slipped to 57.6 this month from a five-year high reading of 58.4 in September. A reading above 50 indicates expansion in the private sector. Strength in manufacturing was offset by a slight pullback in the vast services sector. The PMI suggested the economy started the fourth quarter on solid footing following what is expected to have been a strong performance in the July-September quarter. ... The economy has so far not shown any signs of buckling under the weight of the oil price shock stemming from the US-Israeli war with Iran, with savings, generous tax returns in the spring, tariff refunds, a strong stock market performance and corporate profits providing a cushion. Economists warned that the inflation fallout from the drawn-out Middle East conflict was likely to slow consumer spending this quarter. The survey’s measure of new orders received by businesses edged up to 58.2 this month, the highest level since March 2022, from 58.1 in September. ... Its gauge of prices for output rose to 59.8, the highest reading since August 2022, from 58.4 in September. Businesses across manufacturing and services sectors raised prices. Delivery performance by suppliers to manufacturers deteriorated further. The survey’s measure of suppliers’ delivery times dropped to a more than four-year low of 38.1 from 40.9 in September. ... items.title: Democrats still poised to make gains, but poll shows ...
items.excerpt: Democrats retain significant midterm electoral advantages, with key data pointing to them being the favorites to win control of the U.S. House. But, there are indications of why a potential wave could be limited, a new NPR/PBS News/Marist poll finds. The poll also sheds light on the issues driving voters across the ideological spectrum. The cost of living continues to be top of mind overall with a third of people saying they've experienced financial hardship in the past year and 4 in 10 saying their personal finances have gotten worse. "The economy is at the top of my list right now," said Shun Maurice, a 47-year-old from Arizona who participated in the poll. He's an independent who leans toward Democrats and said high food and gas prices are a strain. "They're too expensive for everybody, no matter who you voted for," he said. "They're just too expensive for the American people in general, and I don't like that." Preserving democracy also continues to resonate with Democrats and independents, while immigration is the biggest concern for self-described MAGA supporters. The poll of 1,289 registered voters was conducted Oct. 19-20. When registered voters are mentioned, the margin of error is +/- 3.7 percentage points. When likely voters are mentioned, it is +/- 3.8 points. ### Most don't think Trump is doing a good job and don't like him This was the first survey this cycle that Marist applied a likely voter screen, and on multiple questions, likely voters were — within the margin of error — slightly less likely than registered voters to disapprove of the president. Likely voters overall were also slightly less likely to want Democrats to run Congress. Likely voters are something of a special sauce in polling. Survey researchers apply various metrics — like levels of enthusiasm, past voting history and how important voting is to different respondents — to try to identify the subsample of people who are most likely to vote. ### Trump leans into unprecedented power ahead of midterm elections In this survey, just 38% of registered voters approved of the job President Trump is doing, with 61% disapproving (-23). Likely voters gave him a 40% to 59% rating (-19), still not very good, but even a slight margin can make a difference in how significant the gains either party might make in the election are. That said, an equal share — 53% — of registered and likely voters said they "strongly disapprove" of the job Trump is doing, tied with last month as the highest ever in the poll. Trump's favorability rating is even lower — just 37% of likely voters have a favorable impression of Trump, while 59% have a negative one. ### Democrats retain the edge on the congressional ballot Democrats also had a strong advantage on which party's candidate people said they are more likely to vote for in their district if the election were held today, known as the generic congressional ballot. Among registered voters, it was a 10-point advantage. With likely voters, it was 8 points, still indicative of Democratic gains. When Democrats have had that kind of lead on the congressional ballot, they have historically done very well. On average, it was +7 in 2018 and +12 in 2006. In both years, Democrats won the House with at least 30 seats flipped. But that was before the 2020 Census and ensuing regular redistricting — and the rare, mid-decade redistricting in the last year and a half after Trump asked Republican states to redraw their maps to potentially give Republicans more seats. Though Democrats followed suit, both redistricting periods have tilted congressional seats in Republicans' direction and given them a relative advantage nationally. Perhaps because of some of those structural disadvantages and past performance, there is a notable degree of nervousness among Democrats. While 98% of Democratic likely voters said they would vote for a Democrat, just 81% thought the Democrat would win, a 17-point difference. Republicans were only 10 points less likely to believe their candidate would win. Notably, among independents, a higher share thought the Democratic candidate would win. ... ### Democrats also have the enthusiasm advantage, but there are some caution flags, too Democratic likely voters are 10 points more likely to say they are "very enthusiastic" about voting (71% vs. 61%). That's actually wider than the difference between Democratic and Republican registered voters in the poll. The caution for Democrats, though, is that several of their key pillar groups are not very enthusiastic to vote, and Republicans have closed the gap on who is following the election "very closely." Just 42% of likely voters under 45, 53% of non-white voters and 56% of white women with college degrees said they are "very enthusiastic" to vote. All of those groups disapproved of the job Trump is doing. Compare that to pro-Trump groups — MAGA voters (68%), white women without degrees (66%) and white evangelical voters (61%). For independents, 48% report being very enthusiastic to vote. Traditionally, younger, as well as Black and Latino voters turn out at disproportionately lower rates in midterm elections. But with the realignment under Trump, more white, college-educated voters are voting Democratic and, as a group, they turn out at the highest rates. When it comes to paying close attention, last month just 34% of registered Republicans said they're following the election very closely, compared to 42% of Democrats. Now, they're even – 46% of Democrats and 45% of Republicans said they're paying very close attention. When it comes to likely voters, there's no difference either – 51% of Democrats to 50% of Republicans. On the positive side for Democrats: those who voted for Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024 are 15 points more likely than Trump 2024 voters to say they are very enthusiastic. And Democrats overall have an 8-point advantage over Republicans when it comes to who cares a "great deal" about who controls Congress. ### Most are confident elections will be fair and accurate, but Republicans lag Three-quarters of likely voters are confident that their state and local governments will run a fair and accurate election. That includes solid majorities of Democrats (88%), Republicans (68%) and independents (75%), but Republicans were 20 points less likely than Democrats to think they would be run well. MAGA supporters were almost 30 points less likely. ... Large majorities also said their preferred candidate should accept the results of the election. That included 70% of Republicans, but again, they were 20 points less likely than Democrats to say they should accept the results. A quarter of Republicans said their candidate should probably or definitely challenge the results.

items.excerpt: # AP Entertainment SummaryBrief at 5:37 a.m. EDT - AP - Oct 27, 2026 - 1 hr ago - 0 - 4 min to read Jay-Z picks himself to headline the Super Bowl halftime show at SoFi Stadium in Southern California LOS ANGELES (AP) — Jay-Z will headline the Super Bowl halftime show on February 14 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California. The NFL, Apple Music, and Roc Nation announced the news Monday night. NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell said he always wanted Jay-Z to perform when the time felt right. Jay-Z expressed excitement about the opportunity, calling it a dream come true. His Roc Nation has partnered with the NFL since 2019 to produce entertainment presentations, including the halftime show. Jay-Z, who has won 25 Grammy Awards, will perform at the stadium where he recently celebrated the 30th anniversary of his debut album, “Reasonable Doubt.” NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Taylor Swift has been inducted into the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame, alongside Lyle Lovett, Shawn Camp, Lee Thomas Miller, Bruce Channel and J.I. Allison. Swift signed her first publishing deal in Nashville at the age of 14. She returned to the city on Monday during the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame annual gala celebration. She said it was an incredible honor to be inducted and described soaking up the lessons from other writers like a sponge. Also honored was country music icon George Strait with the organization's Career Maker Award. He said the songwriters helped to make his career. TOKYO (AP) — Tetsuya Chiba, a legendary Japanese manga artist best known for his boxing series “Ashita no Joe,” or “Fighting for Tomorrow,” has died. He was 87. Chiba’s masterpiece “Ashita no Joe” series, depicting an aspiring young generation during Japan’s postwar era, became a national sensation. The series was so popular that fans even attended a mock funeral for the protagonist’s rival. Chiba was also a vocal supporter of peace and freedom of expression, telling stories of his harrowing memories of war as a child in his autobiographical stories and manga. Chiba’s publisher, Kodansha Ltd., said Tuesday that the artist died at a Tokyo hospital last Thursday. LOS ANGELES (AP) — Actor Walter Koenig, known for playing Ensign Pavel Chekov on “Star Trek,” has died at 90. His talent agent confirmed he passed away Monday at his home in Los Angeles. Koenig's role as Chekov showcased a future where rival nations worked together. “Star Trek” aired from 1966 to 1969 and gained a massive fan following. Koenig's castmate George Takei praised him as a writer, teacher, and friend. Koenig appeared in seven “Star Trek” movies and wrote a book about the series. He also acted in “Babylon 5” and ventured into computer games. NEW YORK (AP) — Ministry, the pioneering industrial rock band that paved the way for acts like Nine Inch Nails, is calling it quits after 45 years. Founder Al Jourgensen confirms the band is done after releasing their 17th album, “Hate To Go — Take Out Or Delivery,” on Oct. 30. A farewell tour will follow. Jourgensen told The Associated Press he believes it's time for a new generation to take over. The final album reflects their multidecade run without leaning into nostalgia and utilizes artificial intelligence in unsettling and surprising ways. Jourgensen jokes about retiring to herd goats and denies wanting a lasting legacy. “We did what we could,” he says of his band. LONDON (AP) — Chris Brown has avoided prison time for beating a music producer with a tequila bottle at a London nightclub three years ago. On Monday, a court gave him an eight-month sentence, suspended for a year. Brown, 37, faced up to three years in prison after pleading guilty to affray in July. The incident occurred at Tape, a private club in Mayfair, in February 2023. Affray involves unlawful violence that causes fear for safety. Brown's plea deal led prosecutors to drop more serious charges. He was arrested in May 2025 after returning to the UK for a concert. A new docuseries about Matthew Perry and the latest Minions movie are among the new streaming releases this week. The Minions return in “Minions & Monsters,” where they become silent movie stars in the 1920s. On Paramount+, “Hanging by a Wire” chronicles a dramatic 2023 rescue in Pakistan. Daddy Yankee releases a new album, “La Postal,” exploring themes of love. Nickelback and Dustin Lynch also have new albums out. On Netflix, a docuseries on Matthew Perry premieres Tuesday. “The Gilded Age” returns for its fourth season on HBO Max. Plus, the video game “Phantom Blade Zero” debuts Thursday. ... NEW YORK (AP) — The iconic musical "Rent" is celebrating its 30th anniversary with a special benefit performance. Original cast members, including Idina Menzel and Anthony Rapp, are returning to the stage Monday. The event will be livestreamed, with proceeds going to Broadway Cares/Equity Fights AIDS. "Rent," inspired by Puccini’s “La Boheme,” explores themes of poverty, drug use, and AIDS in New York's East Village. It won multiple Tony Awards and a Pulitzer Prize. Rapp says the show has inspired many modern musicals and continues to resonate with audiences. Jonathan Larson, the creator, died in 1996 before seeing its success. NEW YORK (AP) — DC Studios scored a modest, R-rated win with “Clayface,” landing a $24 million opening weekend, according to studio estimates Sunday. But the biggest success story in theaters remained A24’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything,” which pulled in $19.5 million in its first weekend of wide release. The Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim-directed “You Can See Everything” increased from 855 locations to 2,655. In expansion, it continued to blow away expectations. With $45.1 million in two weeks, it already ranks among the highest grossing documentaries ever. Ticket sales were also good for the stop motion animation “Wildwood” and the comic fable “Wicker.” But “Ali G: Who Iz I?” was a nonevent in cinemas.
